## 1.1 · UI and UX

| | User interface (UI) | User experience (UX) |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | What is seen and touched: layout, colours, controls | What a person perceives and feels when using the product |
| Question | How does it look? | Was the task done, and how did it feel? |
| Judged by | Looking at it | Watching people use it, and measuring |

The user interface is one part of the experience. Response times, error messages, the API behind the screen and the rules of the game are other parts.


## 1.2 · Three levels of design

| Level | Meaning | What happens | In this lecture |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Visceral** | From *viscera*, the inner organs: a gut feeling, before any thinking | An immediate reaction to how it looks | The user interface |
| **Behavioural** | The behaviour of the person: what is done with the product | Using it: is the task understood, done, under control? | Usability: most of the lecture |
| **Reflective** | Thinking back: conscious thought about the product | What is remembered and told to others afterwards | The end of a game |

D. Norman, *Emotional Design*, 2004.

## 1.3 · Which one is easier to use?

::: {.ux-example name="first-screen" height="305"}
:::

The better-looking interface is rated as easier to use, before it is used.[^aesthetic] An opinion of a page is formed in about 50 ms.[^50ms]

[^aesthetic]: N. Tractinsky, A. S. Katz, D. Ikar, ["What is beautiful is usable"](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0953-5438(00)00031-X), Interacting with Computers 13(2), 2000.
[^50ms]: G. Lindgaard, G. Fernandes, C. Dudek, J. Brown, ["Attention web designers: You have 50 milliseconds to make a good first impression!"](https://doi.org/10.1080/01449290500330448), Behaviour & Information Technology 25(2), 2006.

## 1.4 · Why looks mislead

| Reason | What happens |
|---|---|
| **Looks are the only evidence** | Before use, nothing else can be judged |
| **The halo effect** | One good quality spills over to the others: what is beautiful is taken to be good |
| **Easy to see feels easy to use** | A clear screen takes little effort to perceive, and that ease is felt as simplicity |
| **A good mood forgives** | After a pleasant first impression, small problems feel smaller[^emotional] |

Not always: beauty is linked more to how pleasant a product is than to how usable.[^hassenzahl]

[^emotional]: D. Norman, *Emotional Design*, 2004, chapter 1, "Attractive things work better".
[^hassenzahl]: M. Hassenzahl, ["The interplay of beauty, goodness, and usability in interactive products"](https://doi.org/10.1207/s15327051hci1904_2), 2004.

## 1.5 · Usability can be measured

Usability is defined by three properties, each of them measurable[^iso-11]:

| | Question | Metrics |
|---|---|---|
| **Effectiveness** | Is the goal reached, completely and correctly? | Completion rate, attempts per game |
| **Efficiency** | At what cost? | Time on task, key presses, clicks |
| **Satisfaction** | How does the person feel about it? | Seen in behaviour: second-game rate |

[^iso-11]: ISO 9241-11:2018, *Usability: Definitions and concepts*: "the extent to which a system, product or service can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction in a specified context of use".

## 1.6 · Where it fits in the design process

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[Empathize] --> B[Define]
    B --> C[Ideate]
    C --> D[Prototype]
    D --> E[Test]
    E --> A
    classDef focus stroke-width:3px
    class D,E focus
```

- Design thinking is one of several descriptions of the same loop. Others: the *Double Diamond* (Design Council), *Inspire, Ideate, Implement* (IDEO).
- All of them are loops: a design is a hypothesis until it is tested with people.
- This lecture covers the last two steps: what to build so that it can be used, and how to tell that it worked.

## 2.1 · The Model Human Processor

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    Senses([Eyes, ears]) --> P["Perceptual processor<br/>~100 ms per cycle"]
    P --> WM[("Working memory<br/>~4 chunks")]
    LTM[("Long-term memory")] <--> WM
    WM <--> C["Cognitive processor<br/>~70 ms per cycle"]
    C --> M["Motor processor<br/>~70 ms per cycle"]
    M --> Hands([Hands])
```

A person described like a computer: three processors and two memories, each with measured limits. One cycle of each takes about 240 ms: the time needed to press a key when a light turns on.

## 2.2 · The limits are known

| Limit | What is known[^mhp] | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Perception | Events under ~100 ms apart are seen as one | A response within 0.1 s feels instant |
| Working memory | About 4 chunks, lost within seconds | Show it, do not make people remember it |
| Decision | Time grows with the number of choices, logarithmically | Fewer, clearer choices |
| Movement | Far and small targets take longer | Large targets, close to the hand |

[^mhp]: S. K. Card, T. P. Moran, A. Newell, *The Psychology of Human-Computer Interaction*, 1983: the source of all four limits.
[^cowan]: N. Cowan, ["The magical number 4 in short-term memory"](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0140525X01003922), Behavioral and Brain Sciences 24(1), 2001.

## 2.3 · The action cycle

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    Goal((Goal)) --> Plan --> Specify --> Perform --> System[(System)]
    System --> Perceive --> Interpret --> Compare --> Goal
    classDef execution fill:#e8f0fb,stroke:#1f5fbf,color:#1d2329
    classDef evaluation fill:#e9f6ec,stroke:#1a7f37,color:#1d2329
    class Plan,Specify,Perform execution
    class Perceive,Interpret,Compare evaluation
```

Every interaction is a trip around this cycle.[^action-cycle] It can fail in two places only:

- **Gulf of execution** (plan, specify, perform): the person cannot work out how to do what they want.
- **Gulf of evaluation** (perceive, interpret, compare): the person cannot tell what the system did.

[^action-cycle]: D. Norman, *The Design of Everyday Things*, revised edition, 2013.

## 2.4 · The cycle in the word game

| Part | What is known | Problems in the word game |
|---|---|---|
| **Execution: plan** | 3&nbsp;·&nbsp;Mental models<br>4&nbsp;·&nbsp;People want to start | Hidden rules, the email wall |
| **Execution: specify, perform** | 5&nbsp;·&nbsp;Grouping<br>6&nbsp;·&nbsp;Movement and choice<br>7&nbsp;·&nbsp;Slips and mistakes | No clear next step, the mouse is required, answers lost in one click |
| **Evaluation: perceive** | 8&nbsp;·&nbsp;Attention is narrow<br>9&nbsp;·&nbsp;Three limits of waiting | One result for three words, silent failure, an invisible time limit |
| **Evaluation: interpret** | 10&nbsp;·&nbsp;Errors: explained or repeated | One message for every error |
| **Reflective: the ending** | 11&nbsp;·&nbsp;The peak and the end | An ending without a next step |

::: {.notes}
What is known, in one sentence each:

- **Mental models**: people plan with a model of the system built only from what the screen shows; a rule that is not shown is not known.
- **Starting at once**: people act before they read; anything asked before the first value is a cost that loses people.
- **Grouping**: things that are close together or look alike are seen as belonging together.
- **Emphasis**: one thing that differs is found at once; when many things differ, nothing stands out.
- **Movement**: pointing takes longer the farther and smaller the target is; a key under the finger needs no pointing.
- **Slips**: the plan is right, the action is wrong; they are made hard to do and easy to undo.
- **Narrow attention**: changes outside the focus of attention are missed, so feedback goes where the eyes already are.
- **Limits of waiting**: 0.1 s feels instant, 1 s keeps the train of thought, 10 s is the limit of attention.
- **Errors explained or repeated**: a mistake comes from a wrong model; a message that does not correct the model leads to the same mistake again.
- **The peak and the end**: an experience is remembered by its most intense moment and by how it ended.
:::

## 3.1 · Mental models

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    D["Designer's model<br/>(the code, the rules)"] -->|is built into| S["System image<br/>(what the screen shows)"]
    S -->|is learned from| U["User's model<br/>(what the person believes)"]
    D -.-|no direct line| U
```

- The designer's model becomes the screen; the user's model is learned from the screen alone.
- The two never talk to each other: the screen is the only channel.
- A rule that is in the code but not on the screen never reaches the user's model.


## 3.2 · Hidden rules

::: {.ux-example name="weekend" before="No rules on the screen: the XP per word, the time limit and the weekend bonus live only in the code" after="The rules are shown before the game starts, today's bonus included" try="Find out how much XP a game gives today (a Saturday)" principle="Only what is shown becomes part of the user's model" metric="Weekend return rate"}
:::

## 4.1 · People want to start

- People do not read first and act later: they start at once, and learn while doing.
- The goal of the player is to play. Anything asked before that is a cost paid before any value is seen.
- Every step before the first value loses a share of the people.


## 4.2 · The email wall

::: {.ux-example name="first-screen" height="420" before="An email is required before anything else can be done" after="Play starts a game at once; the email is asked after a win, to keep the XP" try="Start a game" principle="Value first, cost later: the email is asked when there is experience to keep" metric="Start rate"}
:::

## 5.3 · No clear next step

::: {.ux-example name="started" before="Two forms, two equal buttons, labels stacked above the fields" after="One card for the game, the words aligned with their answers, one primary button" try="Find the next step" principle="Related things grouped; one primary action per screen" metric="First-click success"}
:::

## 5.4 · Primary button: left or right?

| Where | Primary button |
|---|---|
| Windows dialogs | First: OK, then Cancel |
| macOS and iOS dialogs | Last: Cancel, then OK |
| Steps of a flow | Next on the right, in reading direction |
| Web forms | No platform rule; often aligned with the fields |

- Neither order is better: users trip on a button that is not where habit expects it.[^ok-cancel] Follow the platform, and be consistent.
- A primary button is found by how it looks, not where it is: it is the one that stands out.

[^ok-cancel]: J. Nielsen, ["OK–Cancel or Cancel–OK? The trouble with buttons"](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/ok-cancel-or-cancel-ok/), Nielsen Norman Group, 2008.

## 6.1 · Movement and choice

```{=html}
<svg viewBox="0 0 900 190" style="width: 100%; max-height: 230px" role="img" aria-label="A small far target and a large near target">
  <g font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="18" fill="#55606b">
    <path d="M40 60 l0 34 l9 -8 l7 15 l6 -3 l-7 -15 l12 -1 z" fill="#1d2329"/>
    <line x1="80" y1="80" x2="740" y2="80" stroke="#9aa5b1" stroke-dasharray="6 6"/>
    <rect x="745" y="68" width="46" height="24" rx="4" fill="#b3261e"/>
    <text x="400" y="65" text-anchor="middle">far and small: slow</text>
    <path d="M40 130 l0 34 l9 -8 l7 15 l6 -3 l-7 -15 l12 -1 z" fill="#1d2329"/>
    <line x1="80" y1="150" x2="200" y2="150" stroke="#9aa5b1" stroke-dasharray="6 6"/>
    <rect x="205" y="122" width="190" height="56" rx="6" fill="#1a7f37"/>
    <text x="420" y="156">near and large: fast</text>
  </g>
</svg>
```

| | Law | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Pointing at a target[^fitts-hci] | <span style="white-space: nowrap">T = a + b · log₂(D / W + 1)</span> | T: time to point; D: distance; W: width of the target; a, b: constants measured for a device |
| Choosing between n options | <span style="white-space: nowrap">T = b · log₂(n + 1)</span> | T: time to decide; n: number of equally likely options; b: a constant measured for a person |

The fastest target is the one that needs no pointing at all: the key under the finger.

[^fitts-hci]: The form used in human-computer interaction: I. S. MacKenzie, ["Fitts' law as a research and design tool in human-computer interaction"](https://doi.org/10.1207/s15327051hci0701_3), Human-Computer Interaction 7(1), 1992.

## 6.2 · The mouse is required

::: {.ux-example name="keyboard" before="Nothing is focused: the mouse is needed for the email, for each new game and for the first word" after="Play and then the first word are focused; Enter moves to the next word and submits after the last" try="Click into a version, then play with the keyboard only" principle="No pointing is the fastest pointing" metric="Key presses and clicks per game"}
:::

## 7.1 · Slips and mistakes

- **Slip**: the right intention, the wrong action. Meaning to click "Submit", hitting "Start game", losing the answers.
- **Mistake**: the action is as intended, but the intention is wrong. Believing there is no time limit, taking a break, coming back to a lost game.

| | Slip | Mistake |
|---|---|---|
| Cause | Habit, attention elsewhere | A wrong mental model (3&nbsp;·&nbsp;Mental models) |
| Happens to | Experts too | Anyone the system did not explain itself to |
| Design answer | Hard to do, easy to undo | Show how the system works |

Errors are not carelessness: their kinds are known and can be designed for.


## 7.2 · Answers lost in one click

::: {.ux-example name="restart" before="“Start game” replaces the words and clears the typed answers without asking" after="“New words” asks first, and only when answers were typed" try="Ask for a new game" principle="Slips are made hard to do and easy to undo" metric="Restart rate"}
:::

## 7.3 · Confirm only when needed

- A confirmation on every action is clicked through without reading: it becomes part of the action.
- Where an action can be undone, undo is better than a question.
- The words of a game cannot be brought back, so a question is asked: once, and only when answers were typed.

## 8.1 · Attention is narrow

- A change outside the centre of attention is easily missed, even a large one.
- People busy with a task do not notice what they are not looking for.[^gorillas]
- Feedback belongs where the eyes already are: at the thing that was just typed or clicked.

[^gorillas]: D. J. Simons, C. F. Chabris, ["Gorillas in our midst: Sustained inattentional blindness for dynamic events"](https://doi.org/10.1068/p281059), Perception 28(9), 1999.

## 8.2 · One result for three words

::: {.ux-example name="wrong-word" before="One message for the whole game, below the form" after="Every word is marked; the cursor moves to the word to fix" try="Submit both: one word has a typo" principle="Feedback where the eyes already are" metric="Attempts per game"}
:::

## 9.1 · Three limits of waiting

| Response within | How it is felt | What the user interface owes |
|---|---|---|
| **0.1 s** | Instant: "I did it" | Nothing |
| **1 s** | A delay, but the train of thought holds | A sign that the action was taken |
| **10 s** | Attention is at its limit | Progress, and a way out |

The limits have been described since 1968.[^response-times] Users prefer a system that shows progress while they wait.

[^response-times]: J. Nielsen, ["Response time limits"](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/response-times-3-important-limits/), Nielsen Norman Group, 1993.

## 9.2 · Silent waiting, silent failure

::: {.ux-example name="slow-network" before="Nothing changes while waiting, and a failed request shows nothing at all" after="“Checking…” at once, “Still checking…” after 1 s, an error that keeps the answers" try="Submit both: the server is slow and the first request fails" principle="Show that work is in progress after 1 s; never fail silently" metric="Silent-failure rate"}
:::

## 9.3 · Every request has four states

| State | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Waiting, under 1 s | Nothing changes | The button says "Checking…" and is disabled |
| Slow, over 1 s | Nothing changes | "Still checking…" |
| Failed | Nothing changes | What happened, and the typed answers are kept |
| Done | The result | The result |

The happy path is one state of four. The other three are designed, or they are left to chance.

## 9.4 · An invisible time limit

::: {.ux-example name="time-limit" before="The limit is not shown; a late answer is reported as wrong" after="A countdown that turns red, and “Time ran out” the moment it ends" try="Wait for 20 seconds, then submit both" principle="Visibility of system status" metric="Expired-game rate"}
:::

## 10.1 · Errors: explained or repeated

- An error message is read at the worst moment: something did not work, and the person is not sure why.
- A mistake comes from a wrong model of the system. A message that does not correct the model leads to the same mistake again.
- A useful message names what happened, says what it means for the person, and offers the next step.[^heuristics]


## 10.2 · One message for every error

::: {.ux-example name="lost-game" before="Correct answers are reported as wrong" after="The real cause, what it means, and a “New game” button" try="Submit both: every answer is correct, but the server has lost the game" principle="A message per cause, with the next step" metric="Completion rate"}
:::

## 10.3 · Four causes, four messages

| Cause | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| A wrong word | "Some translations are wrong, try again" | "2 of 3 correct. Fix the marked word and check again." |
| The time is over | "Some translations are wrong, try again" | "Time ran out. These words can no longer be checked. No experience was lost." |
| The game is lost | "Some translations are wrong, try again" | "This game is no longer available. Saved experience is safe." |
| No connection | Nothing | "Could not reach the server. Your answers are kept." |

"Try again" can never work for the second and the third cause.

## 10.4 · The API limits the screen

| | API before | API after |
|---|---|---|
| Result | One yes or no for the whole game | A result for every word |
| Failure | Every failure is "no" | Each cause has its own status code |
| Rules | Only in the code | Sent to the user interface |
| Player | An email is needed to start | A game is played first, its experience claimed afterwards |

Half of the fixes in this lecture needed the API to change, not only the screen.

## 11.1 · The peak and the end

- An experience is judged afterwards by its most intense moment and by its end, not by the average and hardly by its length.[^peak-end]
- Effort grows as a goal gets closer: customers of a café bought coffee more often the closer they were to a free one.[^goal-gradient]
- The last screen decides whether there is a next time.

[^peak-end]: D. Kahneman, B. L. Fredrickson, C. A. Schreiber, D. A. Redelmeier, ["When more pain is preferred to less: Adding a better end"](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9280.1993.tb00589.x), Psychological Science 4(6), 1993.
[^goal-gradient]: R. Kivetz, O. Urminsky, Y. Zheng, ["The goal-gradient hypothesis resurrected: Purchase acceleration, illusionary goal progress, and customer retention"](https://doi.org/10.1509/jmkr.43.1.39), Journal of Marketing Research 43(1), 2006.

## 11.2 · An ending without a next step

::: {.ux-example name="ending" before="The words disappear; only the XP total is left" after="A summary, progress to the next level, and “Play again” focused" try="Submit both, then play again" principle="Design the end; show the distance to the next goal" metric="Second-game rate"}
:::

## 12.1 · Ten usability heuristics

Jakob Nielsen's list (1994): ten rules of thumb distilled from 249 usability problems found in real projects.

| | Heuristic | In the word game |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Visibility of system status | The countdown, "Checking…" |
| 2 | Match between the system and the real world | "10 XP per word", in the words of the player |
| 3 | User control and freedom | "Keep playing", "Not you?" |
| 4 | Consistency and standards | Enter submits; one look for the primary button |
| 5 | Error prevention | An empty word is caught before it is sent |

***

| | Heuristic | In the word game |
|---|---|---|
| 6 | Recognition rather than recall | The rules on the screen, the remembered email |
| 7 | Flexibility and efficiency of use | A whole game from the keyboard |
| 8 | Aesthetic and minimalist design | One primary action per screen |
| 9 | Help users recognize, diagnose and recover from errors | A message per cause, with the next step |
| 10 | Help and documentation | None needed: the rules fit on the first screen |

## 12.2 · Where the heuristics come from

- The list is a summary of data: a factor analysis of 249 usability problems found in real projects.[^heuristics]
- Each heuristic belongs to a side of the action cycle: roughly, 1 and 9 close the gulf of evaluation, 2 to 8 the gulf of execution.
- **Heuristic evaluation**: a few people go through every screen with the list. It is cheap and finds many problems, but only the ones the reviewers can imagine.

[^heuristics]: J. Nielsen, ["Enhancing the explanatory power of usability heuristics"](https://doi.org/10.1145/191666.191729), CHI '94; the list itself: ["10 usability heuristics for user interface design"](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/ten-usability-heuristics/).

## 12.3 · Where the science is weaker

| Often repeated | What the research says |
|---|---|
| "No more than 7 ± 2 menu items" | The number is about recalling items from memory; a menu is on the screen. Newer estimates of the capacity are about 4.[^cowan] |
| "More choice makes people give up" | The famous jam study did not hold up: a meta-analysis of 50 experiments found an average effect of about zero.[^choice-meta] |
| "5 users find 85 % of the problems" | True on average in the projects studied, where one user found 31 % of the problems; the share differs a lot between projects.[^five-users] |

A guideline is treated like a code metric: a reason to look closer, not a verdict.

[^choice-meta]: B. Scheibehenne, R. Greifeneder, P. M. Todd, ["Can there ever be too many options? A meta-analytic review of choice overload"](https://doi.org/10.1086/651235), Journal of Consumer Research 37(3), 2010.
[^five-users]: J. Nielsen, ["Why you only need to test with 5 users"](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/why-you-only-need-to-test-with-5-users/), Nielsen Norman Group, 2000.

## 13.1 · Goal, question, metric

The approach of the [software construction lecture](09-software-construction.qmd#goal-question-metric), applied to the word game: a metric is useful only when it answers a question that matters.

| Goal | Question | Metric |
|---|---|---|
| Visitors become players | How many visitors start a game? | Start rate |
| Players finish the games they start | How many started games are won? | Completion rate |
| Mistakes are easy to fix | How many tries does a game take? | Attempts per game |
| Playing is quick | What does one game cost? | Time on task, key presses, clicks |
| Players come back | Is a second game started? | Second-game rate |

## 13.2 · Three groups of metrics

| | Gulf of execution | Gulf of evaluation | Reflective level |
|---|---|---|---|
| ISO 9241-11 | **Efficiency** | **Effectiveness** | **Satisfaction** |
| Metrics | Time on task, key presses, clicks, first-click success, start rate, restart rate | Completion rate, attempts per game, expired-game rate, silent-failure rate | Second-game rate, weekend return rate |
| Measured by | Events the product logs; time on task also with a stopwatch or a model of the user | Events the product logs | Events the product logs |

No questionnaire is needed: the product logs what players do (a game started, answers checked, a game won), and each metric is computed from those counts.

## 13.3 · The keystroke-level model

| Operator | What it is | Time[^klm] |
|---|---|--:|
| K | A key press of an average typist | 0.28 s |
| P | Pointing at a target with the mouse | 1.10 s |
| B | Pressing and releasing the mouse button | 0.20 s[^kieras] |
| H | Moving a hand between the keyboard and the mouse | 0.40 s |
| M | Mentally preparing the next step | 1.35 s |

The time of an expert is predicted by counting the operators a task needs, before any user is asked.

[^klm]: S. K. Card, T. P. Moran, A. Newell, ["The keystroke-level model for user performance time with interactive systems"](https://doi.org/10.1145/358886.358895), Communications of the ACM 23(7), 1980, figure 1; K is the time of an average non-secretary typist (40 words per minute).
[^kieras]: The 1980 model counts a button press as a key press; the separate value for the mouse button is from D. Kieras, *Using the Keystroke-Level Model to Estimate Execution Times*, University of Michigan, 2001.

## 13.4 · The cost of two games

- The task: win two games in a row, as an expert who knows every answer and never makes a mistake.
- Every key press, click, hand move and mental step of both versions is counted, and timed with the operators above.

| Version | Key presses | Clicks | Hand moves | Mental steps | Predicted time |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Before | 50 | 4 | 5 | 11 | 36.1 s |
| After, as a guest | 36 | 0 | 1 | 8 | 21.3 s |
| After, experience saved | 52 | 1 | 3 | 10 | 30.6 s |

## 13.5 · What the cost shows

- The mouse is not needed any more: 4 clicks and 5 hand moves became 0 and 1.
- Saving the experience still costs an email, but after the first win, not before the first game.
- The numbers are a prediction for an expert. They say nothing about a person who sees the game for the first time.

## 14.1 · Counting in the product

```{=html}
<svg viewBox="0 0 900 314" style="width: 100%; max-height: 340px" role="img" aria-label="A funnel: every step of the game keeps fewer players than the one before">
<g font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="20">
  <rect x="280" y="10" width="560" height="46" rx="6" fill="#1f5fbf"/>
  <text x="250" y="40" text-anchor="end" fill="#1d2329">Page opened</text>
  <text x="560" y="40" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-weight="600">1000</text>
  <rect x="386" y="66" width="347" height="46" rx="6" fill="#1f5fbf"/>
  <text x="250" y="96" text-anchor="end" fill="#1d2329">Game started</text>
  <text x="560" y="96" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-weight="600">620</text>
  <text x="870" y="96" text-anchor="end" fill="#55606b">−38 %</text>
  <rect x="409" y="122" width="302" height="46" rx="6" fill="#1f5fbf"/>
  <text x="250" y="152" text-anchor="end" fill="#1d2329">Answers checked</text>
  <text x="560" y="152" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-weight="600">540</text>
  <text x="870" y="152" text-anchor="end" fill="#55606b">−13 %</text>
  <rect x="445" y="178" width="230" height="46" rx="6" fill="#1f5fbf"/>
  <text x="250" y="208" text-anchor="end" fill="#1d2329">Game won</text>
  <text x="560" y="208" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-weight="600">410</text>
  <text x="870" y="208" text-anchor="end" fill="#55606b">−24 %</text>
  <rect x="496" y="234" width="129" height="46" rx="6" fill="#b3261e"/>
  <text x="250" y="264" text-anchor="end" fill="#1d2329">Second game started</text>
  <text x="560" y="264" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-weight="600">230</text>
  <text x="870" y="264" text-anchor="end" fill="#b3261e" font-weight="600">−44 %</text>
  <text x="870" y="310" text-anchor="end" font-size="15" fill="#55606b">Example numbers. Right: the share lost since the step above.</text>
</g>
</svg>
```

- A funnel: every step loses people. The step that loses the most is where the next design work goes.
- Only the server sees every game, so that is where they are counted: started, won, out of time, with the tries and the time of each.
- In the [monitoring lecture](13-monitoring.qmd) numbers like these are sent to a metrics system and drawn as dashboards.

## 14.2 · Five games, counted

Two games won at the first try, one at the second, one out of time, one abandoned:

| Metric | Value |
|---|--:|
| Games started | 5 |
| Games won | 3 |
| Games out of time | 1 |
| Completion rate | 60 % |
| First-try rate | 67 % |
| Attempts per won game | 1.33 |
| Median time to win | 40 s |

The median is used, not the mean: one player who left for a coffee would move the mean.

## 14.3 · From a goal to a metric: HEART

| | Goal | Signal | Metric |
|---|---|---|---|
| **H**appiness | Playing feels good | A win at the first try | First-try rate |
| **E**ngagement | Players play a lot | Games per visit | Games started per player per day |
| **A**doption | Visitors become players | A first game is started | Start rate |
| **R**etention | Players come back | A game in a later week | Share of players active after 7 days |
| **T**ask success | Players finish the games they start | A started game is won | Completion rate, median time to win |

Developed at Google to choose a few metrics for a product, starting from its goals.[^heart]

[^heart]: K. Rodden, H. Hutchinson, X. Fu, ["Measuring the user experience on a large scale: User-centered metrics for web applications"](https://doi.org/10.1145/1753326.1753687), CHI '10.

## 14.4 · Performance is user experience

| Core Web Vital | What the person notices | Good, for 75 % of visits |
|---|---|---|
| **LCP**, Largest Contentful Paint | When the main content is there | ≤ 2.5 s |
| **INP**, Interaction to Next Paint | How fast the page reacts to a click or a key | ≤ 200 ms |
| **CLS**, Cumulative Layout Shift | Whether things jump while being read or clicked | ≤ 0.1 |

The limits of waiting again, as numbers a browser can measure.[^web-vitals] They are measured with Lighthouse, in the developer tools of Chrome.

[^web-vitals]: Google, ["Web Vitals"](https://web.dev/articles/vitals).

## 15.1 · Goodhart's law, again

>When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.

| Metric | How it is gamed |
|---|---|
| Completion rate | Easier words |
| Second-game rate | The next game starts by itself |
| Retention | Streaks lost after one missed day; notifications that blame |
| Time in the product | A slower, more confusing interface |
| Sign-ups | The email wall is put back |

Designs that work against the person using them are called **dark patterns**; they were found on 11 % of 11 000 shopping websites.[^dark-patterns]

[^dark-patterns]: A. Mathur et al., ["Dark patterns at scale: Findings from a crawl of 11K shopping websites"](https://doi.org/10.1145/3359183), Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction 3(CSCW), 2019.

## 15.2 · What was not measured

- The cost of the task is predicted by a model of an expert. No person was timed.
- The five games of the metrics example are made up, not real players.
- Whether the new messages are understood, and whether the email is given more willingly after a win, is a hypothesis.
- An automatic accessibility check (axe-core) finds no problem in either version: it finds what is broken, not what is unusable.

Models and heuristics find problems cheaply. Only people using the product show whether they were solved.

## 16.1 · Summary

| Level | What is known | Measured as |
|---|---|---|
| **Visceral** | Looks are judged in 50 ms, and bias the judgement of usability | Not a measure of usability |
| **Gulf of execution** | Mental models, grouping, emphasis, movement, slips | Efficiency |
| **Gulf of evaluation** | Narrow attention, limits of waiting, errors explained | Effectiveness |
| **Reflective** | The peak and the end, the goal gradient | Satisfaction |

- People have known limits. An interface is designed for them, or against them.
- Several fixes needed the API to change, not only the screen.
- What is claimed about usability can be measured.

## 16.2 · For the team project

1. The main task of the product is walked through the action cycle: where can a person fail to *do* it, where can they fail to *see what happened*?
1. Three problems are fixed. For each: the stage, the principle, a screenshot before and after.
1. One metric of the product is counted from what users do, not asked.
